learn.title: Levelised Cost of Energy Explained Simply
learn.intro: Levelised Cost of Energy, or LCOE, is the single best metric for comparing different power sources fairly. It bundles every lifetime cost—fuel, construction, operations, decommissioning—into one price per megawatt-hour. This apples-to-apples view is reshaping how nations plan their grids and why renewables are winning globally.
learn.c1_text: LCOE divides a power plant's total lifetime costs by the total electricity it generates over its lifetime, expressed in ₹/MWh or $/MWh. Think of it like calculating the per-kilometre cost of owning a car: include purchase, fuel, maintenance, insurance, then divide by distance driven. Without this, comparing solar to coal is meaningless.
learn.c2_title: Why Renewables Now Beat Fossil Fuels 📉
learn.c2_text: In 2010, solar LCOE was roughly $400/MWh and onshore wind $120/MWh. By 2023, utility solar dropped to about $60/MWh and onshore wind to $50/MWh—below new coal and gas. Falling capital costs, longer plant life, and zero fuel costs drive this curve. Learning curves: every doubling of capacity cuts costs roughly 24%.
learn.c3_text: India's 2023 SECI solar auction cleared at just ₹2.50/kWh (~$30/MWh), among the world's lowest. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy now uses LCOE modelling to justify expanding solar from 90 GW to 500 GW by 2030. However, LCOE misses grid integration costs, which MNRE adds via storage tenders.
learn.stat1: Global: Utility solar LCOE fell 89% from 2010 to 2023
learn.stat2: India: SECI solar auction hit ₹2.50/kWh in 2023

learn.title: How Wind Turbines Generate Clean Electricity
learn.intro: Wind turbines convert moving air into electrical power through elegant aerodynamics and electromagnetic induction. As countries race to decarbonise, understanding turbine mechanics helps communities engage with local wind projects and policymakers plan the offshore wind boom reshaping global energy supply chains.
learn.c1_text: Turbine blades work like aircraft wings inverted: air moves faster over the curved upper surface, creating lower pressure that lifts the blade forward. A cut-in wind speed of just 3-4 m/s begins rotation. Modern 15 MW offshore turbines have 100+ metre blades sweeping areas larger than seven football fields.
learn.c2_title: From Spinning Shaft to Grid Power ⚡
learn.c2_text: Blade rotation turns a low-speed shaft driving a gearbox that spins a high-speed shaft at roughly 1,500 rpm. This drives a generator using electromagnetic induction—magnets rotating inside copper coils push electrons, creating AC power. Power output scales with swept area and wind speed cubed, making size matter enormously.
learn.c3_text: India has 47 GW of installed wind capacity (2024), fourth-largest globally, concentrated in Tamil Nadu and Gujarat. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy runs the Offshore Wind Energy Lease Round targeting 30 GW by 2030 along Tamil Nadu and Gujarat coasts. Monsoon-season winds give India among the world's highest capacity factors.
learn.stat2: Modern offshore turbine rating: 15 MW (Vestas V236)
learn.stat3: Cut-in wind speed for modern turbines: 3-4 m/s

learn.title: Green Steel: Hydrogen Replaces Coal
learn.intro: Steel production currently accounts for 7% of global CO₂ emissions, mostly from coking coal in blast furnaces. Replacing that coal with green hydrogen could decarbonise one of the world's dirtiest industries. Green steel is now central to industrial decarbonisation roadmaps across Europe, Asia, and the G7.
learn.c1_title: The Coal Problem in Blast Furnaces 🏭
learn.c1_text: Traditional blast furnaces use coke, a coal derivative, both as fuel and as a chemical reductant that strips oxygen from iron ore to produce metallic iron. Each tonne of steel emits roughly 1.8 tonnes of CO₂. A typical integrated steel plant releases more CO₂ than entire small countries.
learn.c2_text: Green hydrogen direct reduction replaces coke with H₂ gas. At 800°C, hydrogen strips oxygen from iron ore, producing water vapour instead of CO₂. The resulting 'sponge iron' is then melted in an electric arc furnace powered by renewables. This eliminates 95% of emissions per tonne of steel produced.
learn.c3_text: India is the world's second-largest steel producer at 140 million tonnes annually, projected to reach 300 MT by 2030. The Ministry of Steel's 2023 Green Steel Taxonomy sets interim targets. Tata Steel is piloting hydrogen-based DRI at Jamshedpur. India must balance growth with 45% emissions intensity reduction by 2030.
learn.stat1: Global steel emissions share: 7% of CO₂
learn.stat2: CO₂ per tonne conventional steel: 1.8 tonnes
learn.stat4: Hydrogen DRI emissions reduction: up to 95%

learn.title: Perovskite Solar Cells: Beyond Silicon
learn.intro: Perovskite solar cells represent the most exciting breakthrough in photovoltaics since silicon dominated decades ago. Their tunable bandgap, lightweight flexibility, and rapidly climbing efficiencies promise cheaper, more versatile solar panels that could be printed like newspapers or even coated onto windows and walls.
learn.c1_text: Perovskites are materials with a specific ABX₃ crystal structure—often a hybrid organic-inorganic lead halide. Unlike silicon, they can be tuned chemically to absorb different light wavelengths. Think of silicon as a fixed-recipe bread loaf; perovskites are customisable, with 'ingredients' adjusted for optimal sunlight absorption.
learn.c2_text: Perovskite cell efficiency leapt from 3.8% in 2009 to over 26% in 2024—the fastest improvement of any photovoltaic technology in history. Silicon took 40 years to reach 26%. Tandem cells stacking perovskite on silicon achieve 33.9% efficiency, far beyond silicon's theoretical 29.4% single-junction limit.
learn.c3_text: India's Ministry of New and Renewable Energy launched a ₹47 crore Perovskite Solar Cell R&D programme in 2023. IIT Kanpur and IIT Bombay run pilot lines targeting 20% efficiency on glass substrates. Startups like Solex are developing indigenously manufactured perovskite modules. India's high humidity remains a stability challenge.

learn.title: Microgrids: Local Power, Local Resilience
learn.intro: Microgrids are small, self-contained electrical systems that can operate independently from the main grid. They combine local generation, storage, and smart controls to keep lights on during blackouts and electrify remote villages. As extreme weather increases, microgrids are becoming pillars of energy resilience worldwide.
learn.c1_text: A microgrid bundles distributed generation—solar panels, wind turbines, diesel gensets—with battery storage, smart inverters, and a controller. Think of it as a small-scale power plant that serves a campus, village, or neighbourhood. It can 'island' itself from the main grid within milliseconds during outages, keeping critical loads running.
learn.c2_text: After Hurricane Maria in 2017, Puerto Rico's grid collapsed for months; community microgrids powered hospitals and water pumps. California's wildfire blackouts have accelerated microgrid adoption. Hospitals, military bases, and data centres now deploy microgrids to guarantee uptime, often achieving 99.9% reliability through local generation.

learn.title: EV Charging: Level 1, 2, and DC Fast Explained
learn.intro: Electric vehicle adoption depends on charging infrastructure being as convenient as petrol pumps. Understanding the three charging levels—slow AC, faster AC, and rapid DC—is essential for buyers, fleet operators, and city planners. India's charging network is expanding rapidly under FAME-II and the PM E-Drive scheme.
learn.c1_text: Level 1 uses a standard 230V Indian household socket with the portable cable that ships with most EVs. It delivers roughly 2.3 kW, adding 10-15 km of range per hour—best for overnight top-ups or two-wheeler charging. Think of it as refilling a water tank with a garden hose: slow but works.
learn.c2_text: Level 2 AC charging operates at 7-22 kW using a dedicated wall box or public charger. A Tata Nexon EV charges from 10% to 80% in roughly 6 hours overnight. Most Indian homes and workplaces install Level 2 chargers. It requires three-phase connection but is far cheaper than DC fast hardware.
learn.c3_title: Level 3: DC Fast Charging for Highways 🛣️
learn.c3_text: DC fast chargers bypass the car's onboard AC converter, pumping 50 kW to 350 kW directly into the battery. A 50 kW CCS2 charger adds 200+ km in 30 minutes—ideal for highway corridors. Tata Power and Statiq are building DC fast networks along NH-48 and NH-44 under FAME-II funding.
learn.stat4: India FAME-II EV charging outlay: ₹1,000+ crore
